open-question.question: Cairn's two dispatched agents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter under the plugin's agents/ directory. Codex defines custom subagents as TOML files (name, description, developer_instructions) looked up in the project's .codex/agents/ or the user's ~/.codex/agents/, its documentation does not say a plugin can ship them, and no plugin in its curated marketplace ships one. On Codex, in what form should the plugin carry each agent's instructions, and by what step, if any, should they become subagents a cairn skill can spawn?
open-question.recommendation: It is the only form that rests solely on documented Codex behaviour, with no registration outside the plugin, nothing to go stale on upgrade, and no format conversion in the build, and the one value it adds to the dispatch prompt is a path the subagent has no other way to learn.
open-question.alternative: The plugin carries each agent's instructions as the Markdown file core/ holds, in the tree's agents/ directory. Codex never registers anything: no TOML file and no registration step. On Codex the dispatch sites spawn Codex's default (generic) subagent and give it a prompt that tells it to read and follow the plugin's agent file, using the plugin-root path, followed by the task heading or Short Title as today. It relies only on documented behaviour: Codex spawning a generic subagent. Nothing is written outside the installed plugin, nothing goes stale when the plugin is upgraded, the build needs no format conversion, and the single source of the instructions stays the core/ Markdown file. The agent's frontmatter means nothing on Codex. Its description, any tool restriction, and the alternatives agent's read-only stance are carried only by prose the generic subagent may follow imperfectly. The dispatch prompt gains an instructions path, which shifts the rule that it carries only the heading or Short Title and directory. The two dispatch sites must read differently on Codex, so this depends on the Codex plugin-root literal and on how host-specific wording reaches the tree, both owned by sibling questions.

The plugin carries each agent exactly as core/agents/ holds it: a Markdown file with name and description frontmatter under the tree's agents/ directory, with no Codex-specific file and no new build capability. There is no registration step. Each agent is expected to become spawnable by name because Codex discovers it from the installed plugin's agents/ directory, the way it discovers the plugin's skills/. Nothing changes in the build, core/, or the user's setup. The Codex tree's agents/ directory is the same as on the other two hosts, and installing the plugin is the whole setup. This matches how three curated plugins already ship Markdown agent files with name/description frontmatter. It rests on behaviour Codex's documentation does not state. Its subagents page names only TOML files in ~/.codex/agents/ or .codex/agents/, and no curated manifest declares an agents key. If discovery does not happen, both dispatches fail on Codex, and the goal's two agent dispatches go with them. Whether this holds can only be settled by the live probe whose timing a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: Cairn's skills read the project's environment context from CLAUDE.md, the bootstrap skill writes the Milestone Workflow section into it, and finish-current-milestone updates it, while Codex's project instruction file is AGENTS.md. open-question.recommendation: Codex loads AGENTS.md and its own /init fills it, and a typical Codex project already has one, so this is the only choice where the workflow section reaches every Codex session and the skills read the file the host maintains; it is one file-name substitution, and a mixed-host project can link the two files as this repository does.
open-question.alternative: Only the Codex tree names AGENTS.md in place of CLAUDE.md, everywhere it occurs. Its skills and complete-procedure.md read AGENTS.md for environment context. Its bootstrap creates AGENTS.md or appends the Milestone Workflow section to it and points at Codex's /init, and its finish-current-milestone updates AGENTS.md. It never reads or writes CLAUDE.md. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep CLAUDE.md unchanged. It matches Codex's native convention end to end. The workflow guidance lands in the file Codex loads at session start, Codex's /init fills the same file the skills read, and the other two trees stay as they are. The difference spans ten core/ files and 35 mentions, so it depends on how the sibling host-specific wording question settles. The build's three text operations cannot substitute one filename for another today. A project used from both Claude Code and Codex would hold two separately maintained context files that drift apart. A project bootstrapped from Claude Code and then opened in Codex would have its CLAUDE.md context ignored by the Codex skills.

The Codex tree keeps naming CLAUDE.md exactly as core/ does today, with no host-specific wording and no bridge to AGENTS.md. The skills read it for environment context. init-milestone-base-workflow creates it or appends the Milestone Workflow section to it, and finish-current-milestone updates it. The bootstrap's advice to run /init stays as it is. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees are unchanged. It needs no change to core/ or the build for this point: the 35 CLAUDE.md mentions across ten core/ files render into the Codex tree as they are. The context file stays one file across all three hosts, so a project worked from Claude Code and from Codex shares one environment description. Codex loads AGENTS.md, not CLAUDE.md, as its project instruction file. The Milestone Workflow section the bootstrap writes would therefore never reach a Codex session unless the user links the two files themselves, as this repository does by hand. Codex's own /init writes AGENTS.md, so the bootstrap's "run /init to fill it" advice would fill a file the skills never read, and the skills' "suggest running /init" fallbacks would keep finding CLAUDE.md empty.

Only the Codex tree changes. Its skills and complete-procedure.md read AGENTS.md when it exists and fall back to CLAUDE.md when only that exists. Its bootstrap and finish-current-milestone write to whichever of the two already holds the context, and create AGENTS.md when neither exists, pointing at Codex's /init. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep CLAUDE.md unchanged. A project already bootstrapped from Claude Code, or one that keeps a CLAUDE.md, keeps working when opened in Codex. A fresh Codex-only project still gets the native AGENTS.md. Mixed-host projects end up with one context file rather than two. Every Codex site that names the context file carries a two-file lookup and a write-target rule rather than one filename. When the context sits in CLAUDE.md, Codex itself still does not load it at session start, so the Milestone Workflow guidance reaches Codex's skills but not its general sessions.

The Codex tree keeps CLAUDE.md as the one file its skills read and write, as core/ names it today. Only the Codex bootstrap gains one step: when AGENTS.md does not exist, it creates AGENTS.md as a symlink to CLAUDE.md, the arrangement this repository already uses, and includes it in its commit paths. When AGENTS.md already exists, the bootstrap leaves it untouched. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees are unchanged. One context file serves all three hosts, and Codex loads it natively through the link. The 35 read and update mentions stay as they are, so the host-specific difference shrinks to one bootstrap step. Codex's /init then writes through the link into the same file the skills read. That one bootstrap step still needs host-specific wording, so it depends on how the sibling wording-mechanism question settles. Symlinks degrade to plain text files on checkouts without symlink support, such as Windows with core.symlinks off. A project that already has its own AGENTS.md is left with Codex loading a file the skills never read.

core/ stops naming a file and refers, in every host's tree, to "the project instruction file this host loads at session start". Each runner resolves that to its own host's file: CLAUDE.md on Claude Code, AGENTS.md on Codex, and whatever Antigravity loads. The bootstrap creates or appends to that file, finish-current-milestone updates it, and the /init advice is phrased by capability. The rewording reaches all three trees, along with the docs, the README bootstrap step, and the CLAUDE.md invariant that names the file. It follows the existing core/ rule that host-dependent sentences name the capability, never the host. It needs no new build operation and no host-specific mechanism for this point, and every host gets its native file, Codex included. The text of the Claude Code and Antigravity trees changes, so it is acceptable only under the sibling preservation bar. Correct behaviour depends on each model knowing which file its own host loads, which is unverified for Antigravity and for a Codex subagent. The bootstrap's literal "# CLAUDE.md" template heading and the docs that name CLAUDE.md need rewording, and a mixed-host project still ends up with two files.

open-question.question: docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md documents headless chains as `claude -p` or `agy -p` lines, explains each flag per host, and gives a one-line swap between those two binaries. Codex runs non-interactively as `codex exec` with different flag names and no effort flag. How much Codex coverage should that page gain?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: It gives a Codex user a complete mechanical translation of every chain under the same rule the page already uses for agy, built only from flags the installed CLI's help confirms, and it ships no Codex model id, effort level, or literal line that no run has exercised.
open-question.alternative: Extend "Notation and flags" so that Codex is a third binary: - Name `codex exec "<prompt>"` as the Codex form of a line. - Give each flag its Codex counterpart or say it has none: the permission bypass maps to Codex's own approvals-and-sandbox setting, `--model` has a counterpart in `-m`, `--effort` has no flag, and `--add-dir` exists under the same name. - Extend the one-line swap rule so a line moves to Codex by changing the binary, dropping `--model` and `--effort` to run at the account's defaults (as every agy line already does), and replacing the permission flag. No chain gets a Codex line. Gives a Codex user a complete, mechanical way to translate every chain, using the same rule the page already uses for agy. The page avoids naming any Codex model or effort level that a free-tier account may not offer, and its chains stay one block each. Codex runs lose the page's effort tiers (high, xhigh, max), which the chains deliberately vary line by line. That gap is real, because Codex does accept a reasoning effort through `-c model_reasoning_effort=…`. The swap rule's permission mapping depends on how the "Codex sandbox requirements" question settles, and the prompt text depends on the "Codex skill invocation form" question. No `codex exec` line is shown to have been run.

The page could gain Codex coverage in a later milestone, once a live headless Codex run has shown it works. Publishes nothing about Codex's headless form until it has been run. The milestone goal names Codex coverage in docs/ as part of being release-ready, and this is the only docs page that names host binaries (skill-reference.md mentions hosts only by capability). A Codex user would get no headless form, and the page's claim that a chain can mix hosts line by line would stay limited to two of the three supported hosts.

Add one sentence to the "Notation and flags" section saying that on Codex a headless run is `codex exec` with the prompt as its argument, and that its flags differ, pointing to `codex exec --help`. Add no flag-by-flag mapping, do not extend the swap rule, and add no Codex line to any chain. Every claude and agy line stays unchanged. Meets the goal's "Codex coverage in docs/" at almost no cost and with little that can go stale. The page claims only that `codex exec` exists, which the installed codex-cli 0.159.3 confirms. The user has to work out each flag alone: `-p` means a config profile on Codex, not a prompt, and there is no `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or `--effort`. The swap rule tells the user to carry the line's model and effort over to Codex: a Codex model id through `-m`, and the line's effort through the `-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"` config override, with the legend listing the effort levels Codex accepts. The permission mapping and prompt text depend on the "Codex sandbox requirements" and "Codex skill invocation form" questions.

open-question.question: The alternatives pass dispatches one subagent per open question, all at once where the host allows parallel dispatch and one after another where it does not, with no cap. Codex runs subagents in parallel but limits how many subagent threads a session may hold open at once. How should the pass behave on a host that allows parallel dispatch only up to a limit?

recommendation.option: Sliding window at a stated cap

open-question.recommendation: It gives the pass a defined outcome on a question set larger than the cap without the runner having to provoke and interpret a refusal, uses every free slot as each return lands the way the pass already judges returns, and confines the change to the Codex tree so the other two dispatch exactly as written today.

alternative.id: Sliding window at a stated cap

open-question.alternative: Only the Codex tree's dispatch step names an explicit limit: keep at most the session's configured subagent thread cap in flight at once, as Codex's agents.max_threads setting or the default value the prose states. As each question's pipeline finishes (embedded and committed, or skipped after its one repair), its agent is closed and the next pending question is dispatched. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep the uncapped all-at-once wording unchanged. Repair by continuation is unaffected, because closing waits for the repair window to end. The runner is told the limit up front, so it never has to provoke and interpret a refusal. The other two host trees can stay byte-identical, because the difference is confined to the Codex tree. It needs a way to deliver Codex-only wording into a core/ step. That mechanism belongs to the Host-specific wording mechanism question, and the build today offers only plugin-root replacement, regex deletion, and frontmatter stripping. The stated number can also drift from the user's actual configuration (the setting is user-editable, and Codex refuses agents.max_threads when multi_agent_v2 is enabled). A stated value that is too high brings back the refusal it was meant to avoid, and one that is too low wastes parallelism.

The pass keeps its current wording: every surviving question is dispatched at once where the host can run several dispatches together, with no cap. Neither core/ nor the Codex host definition adds any wording about a thread limit, so on Codex the host's own limit decides what happens to dispatches beyond it. Spawns past the limit get Codex's "agent thread limit reached" refusal, the prose defines no handling for that refusal, and the runner deals with it however it chooses. No thread is closed explicitly. Nothing in core/, the build, or either existing host tree changes. This milestone's live verification dispatches the alternatives agent only once, so it never comes near the limit and the pass works as written for that run. The pass has no defined outcome when a spawn is refused. This milestone alone holds sixteen open questions, well above a typical cap such as the agents.max_threads value Codex reads from config.toml. A refused spawn may be misread as a failure and skipped, may be retried blindly, or may stall the run. If finished subagent threads keep counting against the cap until they are closed (the Codex binary has a close_agent operation), even the sequential arm would hit the cap partway through. That behaviour is unverified, and when to probe it is up to the Unverified behaviour probes question.

The dispatch step in core/ gets host-neutral wording: dispatch together as many questions as the host will accept. A dispatch the host refuses because its agent limit is reached is not a failure and not a skip. It stays pending and is dispatched again as soon as a running question's pipeline has finished (embedded and committed, or skipped after its one repair). Where the host keeps finished agents open, that question's agent is closed at that point, so the window slides one slot at a time. The prose states no number: the window's size is whatever the host accepts. On a host with no limit the refusal never happens and the wording reduces to today's all-at-once arm. Repair by continuing the same session keeps working, because an agent is closed only once its repair window is over. Codex parallelism is used fully up to whatever limit the user's own configuration sets. The prose needs no stated number and no Codex-only sentence, and it reads correctly on every host, so the Claude Code and Antigravity runs dispatch exactly as they do now. The dispatch sentence in core/ changes, so the Claude Code and Antigravity trees change in text though not in behaviour. Whether that is acceptable depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. The approach also depends on the runner recognising the limit refusal as distinct from an agent failure, and on Codex releasing a slot when an agent is closed. Neither is yet confirmed by a live run (see the Unverified behaviour probes question).

The dispatch step in core/ gets host-neutral wording: dispatch questions until the host refuses one because its agent limit is reached, or until none are left. The accepted dispatches form a wave. Each return in the wave is judged, repaired once if needed, and committed or skipped as it lands. When the whole wave is done, every agent in it is closed (where the host keeps finished agents open) and the next wave starts from the remaining questions. The prose states no number, and on a host with no limit the first wave holds every question, which is today's behaviour. The bookkeeping is simpler than a sliding window. The runner tracks one batch at a time and closes agents in one sweep at the end of each wave, while the prose still needs no number and no Codex-only sentence. Within each wave the slowest agent holds up the start of the next wave, so slots sit idle and the wall-clock time falls between a sliding window's and the sequential arm's. Like the sliding window, the wording changes the core/ text of every host tree, which depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. It also relies on the runner recognising the limit refusal and on closing an agent actually freeing a slot, both unconfirmed by a live run.

Only the Codex tree's dispatch step names an explicit wave size: dispatch up to the session's configured subagent thread cap (agents.max_threads, or the default value the prose states). Each return is judged, repaired, and committed or skipped as it lands. When the wave is done, its agents are closed and the next wave of up to the cap begins. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep the uncapped all-at-once wording unchanged. It is the most predictable capped behaviour. The runner knows each wave's size before dispatching, never needs to interpret a refusal, and closes agents in one place. The other two host trees can stay byte-identical. It combines the costs of both of its positions. Slots sit idle while the slowest agent of each wave finishes. It needs the Codex-only wording mechanism that the Host-specific wording mechanism question owns. And the stated size can drift from the user's configured cap or from what multi_agent_v2 enforces.

alternative.id: Capped hosts take the sequential arm

open-question.alternative: The existing sequential arm's condition widens, in host-neutral wording in core/, from "where the host cannot run several dispatches at once" to "where it cannot run several at once, or can run only a limited number". On such a host each question is dispatched, judged, repaired at most once, and committed or skipped before the next is dispatched. Its agent is closed once its question is done, where the host keeps finished agents open. No number is stated and no window or wave is tracked. It reuses an arm the pass already defines, which writes the same blocks and lands the same commits. It adds no new dispatch mechanism and needs no Codex-only sentence. At most one subagent thread is ever open, so the cap cannot be reached whatever the user's configuration, and the one open handle keeps repair by continuation trivial. Total token use is the same as a parallel run. It gives up Codex's parallelism entirely, so a large question set takes as long as the slowest serial run. The arm's condition sentence also changes the core/ text of the Claude Code and Antigravity trees, which depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. And it still relies on closing a finished agent freeing its thread, which is unconfirmed on Codex.

This rejects the premise that the pass should adapt. The dispatch step stays uncapped and unchanged in core/ and in every host tree. Instead, cairn's Codex-facing instructions tell users to raise Codex's subagent thread limit (agents.max_threads in config.toml) high enough to cover the open questions a milestone can hold before they run the alternatives pass. The pass itself never closes threads and never handles a limit refusal. No runtime file changes on any host, so the existing trees are untouched. On a correctly configured Codex session the pass runs in the same all-at-once arm it uses on Claude Code, with full parallelism. Correctness rests on a user setting that cairn cannot check. A question count above the configured value brings back the undefined refusal, and the count a milestone can reach has no upper bound. The setting cannot be used at all once multi_agent_v2 is enabled (Codex rejects agents.max_threads alongside it), and the instruction adds another configuration step to the Codex installation path.
